text:
Overview

International education partnerships are defined as formal arrangements between UK education institutions, organisations or awarding bodies and overseas counterparts that support the delivery, development, recognition or exchange of education, training, research, skills, qualifications, expertise or educational services. These partnerships may include:

collaborative programme delivery

transnational education (TNE)

qualification licensing

joint research

institutional agreements

skills and workforce development initiatives

student or staff mobility

capacity-building activity

This guidance should be applied in a way that reflects the provider’s size, legal form, education type and risk exposure. The practical considerations listed are neither exhaustive nor all strictly required, and may overlap with existing due diligence requirements imposed by partners and funders. His Majesty’s Government (HMG) does not conduct due diligence on behalf of education providers and such providers should make judgements on the proportionality of their risk management based on the information available to them.

This document is a concise risk-management framework. It does not replace legal advice, local professional advice, regulatory requirements, funding conditions, quality assurance obligations, safeguarding duties or providers’ own policies.

Education regulation differs by provider type and across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. For further information, see:

The UK’s International Education Strategy 2026

National Security Strategy 2025

Understand the purpose and policy context

International education is one of the UK’s most important global assets. The UK Government’s International Education Strategy places education – from schools and colleges to universities, training providers, awarding organisations and education businesses – at the heart of the UK’s global engagement. It aims to make the UK the global partner of choice at every stage of learning and to grow the value of education exports to £40 billion a year by 2030.

International partnerships and overseas delivery can:

expand access to high-quality UK education

build long-term relationships

strengthen institutions and skills systems

support growth and influence

The strategy also recognises that sustainable transnational education depends on providers understanding and managing the legal, financial and security risks of operating overseas.

These opportunities sit within a more uncertain geopolitical environment. The National Security Strategy 2025 describes an era of radical uncertainty, intensifying state competition and greater geopolitical volatility. It emphasises resilience, secure and sustainable growth, strong international partnerships and reducing dependencies that could be used for coercive purposes.

Most international education partnerships are legitimate, beneficial and capable of being managed through ordinary governance and due diligence processes. Enhanced scrutiny should be reserved for situations where the scale of activity, nature of the partner, operating environment or potential consequences justify additional assessment.

The purpose of this guidance is not to discourage international engagement, but to support informed decision-making and sustainable partnerships that maintain the highest quality of overseas provision.

Core principle

Effective risk management enables safe and informed international engagement and minimises negative outcomes for providers.

Providers should take a proportionate, evidence-led and whole-lifecycle approach. They should:

understand the opportunity

identify the risks

put workable safeguards in place, or where none are identified, refuse to proceed

monitor change

retain credible options to escalate or exit

Decide when to carry out an enhanced risk assessment

When carrying out an enhanced risk assessment, providers should:

carry out appropriate due diligence before agreeing a partnership

make the assessment proportionate to the provider’s size, type and exposure, and to the proposed partnership

base the depth of due diligence and oversight on the combined risk, scale, nature and potential consequences of the activity, rather than on individual risk factors in isolation

monitor the risk continuously and review it periodically when circumstances change.

Identify when an enhanced risk assessment may be required

There is no fixed list of countries, entities or activities that automatically require an enhanced risk assessment. An entity, relationship, activity or operating environment may warrant additional scrutiny where the characteristics of the partner, the nature of the proposed activity, the location, or the effectiveness of available safeguards increase the likelihood or potential impact of harm. This may include:

harm to the provider, its staff or learners

the quality and integrity of education

UK interests

compliance with legal and regulatory obligations

Risk is contextual and may change over time. A partner operating in a generally less complex environment may still present significant concerns. Equally, engagement in a more complex or sensitive environment may be possible where the benefits are clear, the risks are understood and proportionate safeguards can reduce those risks to an acceptable level. Engagement with a state-linked entity is a normal part of international collaboration but may come with additional risk.

Providers should recognise that not all risks can be adequately mitigated. Where concerns remain outside the organisation’s agreed risk appetite or tolerance, the appropriate response may be to decline, pause, suspend or exit the activity.

Essential risk management considerations

You should:

agree the provider’s risk appetite before conducting any due diligence

assess the partner, activity and operating environment together

record the evidence used, controls proposed, residual risk, who has accepted it and when the assessment will be reviewed

Assess whether the operating environment requires an enhanced risk assessment

This section includes 5 risk dimensions and associated factors.

Security environment

Consider whether:

the proposed partner or activity could create significant access to people, systems, data, intellectual property or wider institutional networks

there is credible evidence of activity by state or state-linked actors intended to:

undermine UK national interests

obtain sensitive knowledge or technology

interfere in decision-making

conduct cyber activity

exert coercive pressure

monitor, intimidate or repress individuals

Political and value environment

Consider whether:

the local approach to free speech, civil liberties, corruption, human rights, equality, academic freedom and institutional autonomy aligns with the provider’s legal and regulatory duties, standards or values

compulsory curriculum or education requirements, censorship, restrictions on discussion, or other expectations placed on staff and learners conflict with those duties, standards or values

Commercial and legal environment

Consider:

how clear, stable and predictably enforced laws and regulations are

whether licences, approvals, payments and income can be secured and remitted

whether courts, arbitration and other dispute mechanisms are sufficiently independent and objective

whether the country has laws or practices that compel entities and individuals to be subject to direction from their governments to provide British information, research knowledge, technology and its resulting intellectual property

contract enforceability, change of law, insolvency, intellectual property, taxation, currency controls and the practical ability to recover money or assets

Safety environment

Consider:

whether the location of the partner institution carries risks, including detention or exit restrictions, surveillance, crime, terrorism, discrimination, civil unrest, health risks and limited consular access

how these risks affect travelling or resident staff and learners

whether particular individuals face greater risk because of their identity, work, previous work or posts held in public or private institutions, access to sensitive information or public profile

whether the provider is adequately prepared to manage these risks and staff are adequately aware of potential risks and contingency plans, where appropriate

Geopolitical environment

Consider:

how likely sudden disruption to policy, regulation, diplomatic relations, sanctions, transport, finance, data flows or supply chains is

whether conflict, political instability or a deterioration in bilateral relations make the provision, contract or physical presence unviable at short notice

Use reliable evidence

Use several current and independent sources. Do not rely only on a partner’s assurances or a single commercial country rating. Sources include:

Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) foreign travel advice – current safety, security, entry, legal and travel warnings.

Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Overseas business risk reports – political, economic, human rights, corruption, security and business-environment information.

the UK Sanctions List – screen relevant entities, individuals and ownership or control relationships.

Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade export support – market intelligence and access to UK teams overseas.

Use independent legal, financial, beneficial ownership, adverse-media and integrity checks proportionate to the risk. Procure third-party due diligence services, ranging from target verification for limited activity to detailed reports for major long-term collaborations or branch campuses.

Where an education partnership involves, enables or could develop into research activity, or provides access to research people, facilities or systems, data or technology, providers should engage relevant research-security processes and specialist advice through HMG’s Research Collaboration Advice Team.

Reassess risk when ownership, leadership, law, regulation, funding, scope or geopolitical conditions change.

Check partnership and contract risks

Review the following considerations before approval and contracting, and revisit them at agreed points throughout the relationship:

understand who you are partnering with

assess benefits, motivations and red lines

manage exposure and dependency

meet legal and regulatory requirements

protect people and their data overseas

protect independent decision making and governance

plan how to escalate, suspend or exit partnerships

Higher-risk indicators should lead to enhanced due diligence, additional controls and more senior approval.

Not all considerations will apply to every partnership activity, and providers should use their judgement to determine what is proportionate to their circumstances.

Decision record

For each material consideration, record:

the evidence

the initial risk

the safeguard or contractual control

the residual risk

the accountable owner

the approval decisions

the next review date and exit triggers

Understand who you are partnering with

A partnership may expose the provider to risks arising not only from the immediate counterparty, but also from its owners, controllers, funders, affiliates and connections to state, defence or security bodies.

Taking reasonable and proportionate steps, using available information, to identify who ultimately influences or benefits from the arrangement is essential to identifying unforeseen legal, reputational, commercial and national security risks.

Consider whether:

you have verified the partner’s legal identity, registration, ownership, delivery structure and control, key decision-makers and financial position

the entity’s and key individuals’ wider activities, interests, funding sources and relationships – including relevant affiliates, agents and subcontractors – are sufficiently transparent

the entity’s relationship with the host government – including state ownership, control, oversight or links to defence, security, intelligence or law enforcement – could create value misalignment, commercial, national security or geopolitical risks, or enable unwanted access to the provider’s people, data, technology, facilities, networks or decision makers

there are credible legal, sanctions, integrity, financial, human rights, cyber, academic or staff and learner welfare concerns involving the entity, its owners, controllers or intermediaries

Practical safeguards

Ensure that you:

verify material claims through primary records and independent sources, applying enhanced due diligence to owners, controllers, key individuals, agents and material subcontractors where appropriate

require declarations and management of conflicts of interest, gifts and outside interests, alongside continuing disclosure, change-of-control and periodic re-screening obligations

use contractual audit and information rights, and require approval at a level proportionate to the risk, with material concerns recorded in the institutional risk register

Assess benefits, motivations and red lines

A clear understanding of each party’s motivations helps providers assess whether the proposed access, influence and benefits are proportionate to the stated educational purpose.

Agreed red lines are important because a partnership may expand over time into areas that expose the provider’s reputation, brand, data, intellectual property, academic activity or institutional autonomy to unacceptable risk.

Consider whether:

you and the partner have clearly documented the intended educational, strategic, financial and public benefits for learners, both providers and their respective nations

you can identify the benefits to the partner and host, their motivations, and any wider benefits they may be seeking – such as access to reputation, networks, talent, research, technology, data or influence

the relationship is genuinely mutual and proportionate, or whether there is a mismatch between its stated purpose and the access, influence or benefit requested

how motivations, benefits and risk balance could change over time, including if income, student numbers, political support or market access are lower than forecast

you have agreed clear red lines on what the partnership will not cover or expand into, including content, appointments, admissions, assessment, research, data, intellectual property, brand use and third parties

Practical safeguards

Ensure that you:

prepare a written benefits and motivations assessment, tested against the access, rights and obligations proposed, with due consideration given to which assets are most sensitive

define the permitted purpose, scope, red lines and use of the provider’s brand, content, data, systems and intellectual property in the contract

use formal change control, fresh due diligence and renewed approval for material expansion, and review the benefit-risk balance at agreed milestones or when circumstances change

Higher Education providers should engage relevant research-security processes and specialist advice through HMG’s Research Collaboration Advice Team.

Manage exposure and dependency

Significant exposure to a single partner, country or operating environment can create leverage that may be used for economic coercion or to pressure a provider to alter institutional decisions, policies, public positions or academic activities. It can also reduce the provider’s freedom to act where sudden suspension or termination of the relationship would create material financial stress, disrupt delivery or leave staff and learners without viable alternatives.

Leverage and dependency may also arise through cumulative exposure across multiple partnerships, campuses, programmes or arrangements.

Consider:

what the provider’s overall exposure to the partner or operating environment is, and whether it could be used to exert pressure, create adverse incentives or constrain independent decisions

the extent of physical and people exposure, including staff, learners, campuses, offices, laboratories, accommodation, equipment and records

whether financial and commercial exposure exists, including income, funding, investments, guarantees, student recruitment, assets, deposits, sunk costs and unrecovered expenditure

the extent to which the provider relies on this partner or operating environment for partnerships, delivery capacity, data, technology, intellectual property, systems or suppliers, and how easily these could be replaced if disrupted

how exposure could grow over time, and the disruption that could result if access, approvals, payments, premises, visas, data or licences were withheld, and what thresholds would make the dependency unacceptable

Practical safeguards

Ensure that you:

maintain an exposure register covering people, physical presence, finance, partnerships, student numbers, data, technology and reputation

set parameters on the acceptable level of exposure and dependency on another provider or country, agree terms for approving expansions to original activity, and establish thresholds for escalation when exposure becomes too high

diversify recruitment, delivery, banking, suppliers or partners where practical, and maintain credible contingencies and financial reserves for disruption or exit

Meet legal and regulatory requirements

International activity can engage overlapping UK and overseas legal and regulatory requirements, some of which may conflict or change during the life of the partnership. Failure to identify and manage these obligations can result in:

unlawful activity

financial penalties

loss of licences or funding

regulatory intervention

harm to staff, learners and the provider’s reputation

Consider:

which UK and overseas laws, regulations, licences, approvals, funding conditions, professional standards, education requirements and quality assurance obligations apply to the activity

conflict between UK and local law, and whether the local legal environment, contract enforcement and dispute-resolution mechanisms are sufficiently clear and reliable

whether you have assessed that sanctions, the National Security and Investment Act, the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme, export controls, visa sponsorship or the Academic Technology Approval Scheme apply

whether personal or sensitive information, technology or systems will be transferred or accessed overseas, and whether appropriate data protection, international-transfer and cyber security controls are in place

whether other relevant obligations and risks have been addressed, including bribery and corruption, anti-money laundering, tax, immigration, employment, equality, safeguarding, intellectual property, insurance, travel and reputation

where overseas researchers, staff, fellows, secondees or visiting practitioners will access facilities, systems or educational activity, have right-to-work, visa, access-control, conflicts-of-interest and safeguarding requirements been addressed

Practical safeguards

Ensure that you:

give a named legal or compliance owner responsibility for an obligations map, evidence of licences, registrations and approvals, and review of regulatory change

obtain independent UK and local legal or regulatory advice where needed, consult the relevant education regulator or authority, and make required approvals conditions precedent to activity or payment

include compliance warranties, information and audit rights, cooperation and termination provisions in the contract – map and minimise data and system access, and do not accept obligations that would breach UK law or regulatory duties

Protect people and their data overseas

Failure to identify, manage and follow relevant legislation relating to the care and safeguarding of children, young or vulnerable learners, including when providing education overseas, could result in:

harm to children or learners

unlawful activity

financial penalties

loss of licences or funding

regulatory intervention

Consider whether:

all safer recruitment practices and vetting have been conducted for all staff, researchers, volunteers, work placements, and staff deployed overseas alone or for short periods, and whether appropriate records have been recorded or kept in accordance with requirements

there are clear internal policies for reporting and managing allegations and a whistleblowing policy

personal records, including safeguarding records, will be accessed or shared, and whether appropriate data protections are in place

the provider has sought advice on its ability to intervene where local requirements or practices differ from UK safeguarding standards

Practical safeguards

Include protections for staff and learner welfare, confidential reporting, whistleblowing and non-retaliation, supported by sufficient audit, inspection, information and access rights.

Protect independent decision making and governance

Partnership structures can create formal or informal routes through which a foreign partner seeks to influence appointments, admissions, curriculum, assessment, research, events or public positions.

Clear governance and retained institutional control help protect educational integrity, academic freedom, freedom of speech and the provider’s ability to make decisions independently.

Consider:

where partnership decisions will be made, who will be involved, and how decisions and their rationale will be recorded

the voting, veto, quorum, appointment, removal and reserved-matter rights that each party holds

who will have the ability to inspect, access data, require improvement and approve key educational leadership appointments, particularly where the UK provider oversees and quality assures rather than operates the provision

whether funding, access, gifts, donations, naming rights, exclusivity or personal relationships give the partner unusual influence over the provider or its wider decisions

who controls key decisions on staffing, appointments, curriculum, content, admissions, assessment, quality, research, events, communications, data and intellectual property, and whether the provider can protect educational and academic integrity

whether formal or informal pressure leads to censorship, self-censorship, monitoring, changes to appointments or admissions, changes to activity scope, suppression of complaints or retaliation, and whether staff and learners can report concerns safely

Practical safeguards

Ensure that you:

define non-delegable decisions and reserved matters that remain under the UK provider’s control

use balanced and transparent governance, with clear terms of reference, conflict of interest declarations, accurate records and all material instructions or changes documented through agreed channels

include protections for educational and academic integrity, staff and learner welfare, confidential reporting, whistleblowing and non-retaliation, supported by sufficient audit, inspection, information and access rights

Plan how to escalate, suspend or exit partnerships

Concerns can develop quickly and may require action before all the facts are known, particularly where staff or learner safety, legal compliance, sanctions, data or educational quality are at risk.

Clear escalation routes and credible suspension and exit arrangements enable providers to act promptly, limit further harm and protect staff, learners, assets and continuity of provision.

Consider:

whether there is a named internal route for staff and learners to report and escalate concerns safely, with clear responsibilities across senior leadership and relevant professional functions

when and how to seek support from the UK government, regulators, funding bodies, law enforcement, insurers, advisers and the UK diplomatic network, including what in-country support may be available – for higher education providers this should include the Academic Interference Reporting Route

whether you have defined clear triggers for enhanced review, remediation, a pause, suspension, non-renewal or termination – including legal or sanctions changes, safety or quality failures, interference, non-payment, cyber incidents, hidden ownership or geopolitical disruption

whether the provider can suspend or exit promptly, without the partner’s agreement where necessary, if the arrangement becomes unlawful, unsafe, unviable or inconsistent with the provider’s red lines

what suspension or exit would mean for staff, learners, applicants, qualifications, data, intellectual property, premises, assets, income, liabilities, litigation and reputation, and whether continuity and transition can be managed

Also consider whether staff are aware of contingency and repatriation plans for staff, academics and students, including any risks linked to an individual’s status.

Practical safeguards

Ensure that you:

agree and test an exit plan before signature, including teach-out or transfer arrangements for learners and safety, travel, immigration, employment and repatriation plans for staff

include clear suspension and termination rights, sanctions and change-of-law clauses, change-of-control provisions, audit and information rights, force majeure, transition arrangements and enforceable dispute-resolution provisions

plan how data, systems, equipment, intellectual property, funds, liabilities, premises and supplier arrangements will be recovered or unwound, and pre-agree responsibilities for communications during escalation or exit

Monitor the partnership and maintain oversight

Continue due diligence after deciding to proceed. Manage risks throughout the relationship and review them periodically. Changes in one area of a provider’s activity may create vulnerabilities in another.

Consider whether:

there is a senior accountable owner and a cross-functional team with the authority and information needed to oversee the arrangement

the arrangement is recorded in the appropriate risk register, with material risks reported to the governing body or equivalent oversight body

the partner, owners and controllers, financial position, sanctions status, local environment and compliance position are reviewed at a frequency proportionate to risk

staff and learners are receiving proportionate briefing and training on travel, cyber, data, safeguarding, academic or educational integrity and reporting concerns

internal and confidential reporting routes for concerns by staff and learners have been appropriately advertised and the senior accountable owner of this arrangement is part of the reporting route’s escalation process

controls are being tested in practice – for example audit rights, data restrictions, governance procedures, complaints routes and exit arrangements

there are trigger-based reviews for changes in law, ownership, leadership, scope, student numbers, financial exposure, political conditions or partner behaviour

Each review results in a clear decision:

continue

continue with new conditions

pause

remediate

suspend

do not renew

exit

Governance test

Providers should be able to explain not only why they entered a partnership, but why it remains in their interests and how they know the safeguards are working.

Choose an appropriate decision outcome

The 4 decision outcomes are:

proceed: the benefits to the provider and UK are clear and evidenced, risks are judged to be low or well controlled, legal and regulatory requirements are met, and monitoring and exit arrangements are credible

proceed with conditions: the activity is worthwhile but requires enhanced due diligence, specific contractual protections, limited scope, staged investment, senior approval or more frequent review.

pause and seek advice: the level of risk is unclear because relevant information is missing, the provider’s legal position is uncertain, effective mitigations are not yet practicable, or specialist government, regulatory, security or local advice is needed

do not proceed or exit: the activity is unlawful, benefits do not justify the residual risk, red lines would be breached, staff or learners cannot be protected, or the provider lacks a credible ability to oversee the arrangement or exit safely

Use further sources and support

The following resources provide more detailed guidance.

Providers should use the latest version and select sources relevant to their activity, provider type and UK nation.

UK government strategy and policy

The UK’s International Education Strategy 2026 (all providers)

Government ambitions for international education, TNE and education exports, including the need to understand legal, financial and security risks.

Advancing Talent with UK Education: Building Global Partnerships 2026 (all providers)

Aligned with the UK International Education Strategy 2026, this brochure highlights how the UK brings its commitment to global collaboration to life through the strategy’s three central pillars.

National Security Strategy 2025 (all providers)

Strategic context on geopolitical volatility, resilience, international partnerships, dependencies and coercion.

UK government advice on international business and travel

Overseas business risk reports (all providers)

Country-level information on political, economic, security, corruption, human rights and commercial risks.

FCDO foreign travel advice (all providers)

Current travel, safety, security, legal, health and entry information, with email alerts.

UK sanctions guidance and UK sanctions list (all providers)

Current sanctions guidance, regimes, reporting routes and access to the searchable UK sanctions list.

Higher education-specific resources

Protecting UK higher education from foreign interference (HE)

Recognising, preventing and reporting foreign interference; protecting people, research and academic freedom; regulatory routes across the UK.

Universities UK: managing risks in internationalisation (HE)

Detailed sector guidance on governance, due diligence, people, overseas activity, cyber security, academic freedom, research, intellectual property (IP) and TNE.

Universities UK: managing risk and developing responsible TNE partnerships (HE and TNE)

Integrated lifecycle approach covering financial, reputational, academic freedom, security, relationship, personnel, cyber, data and IP risks.

Office for Students: TNE – protecting the interests of students taught abroad (HE in England)

The Office for Students’ approach to overseas provision and expectations that students registered with English providers receive the required quality and standards.

The Quality Assurance Agency (QAA) UK TNE Quality Scheme (HE and TNE)

Sector-led support for quality, student experience, due diligence and sustainable TNE partnerships.

QAA Quality Code: principle 8 – operating partnerships with other organisations (HE and TNE)

Principle 8 covers the arrangements for maintaining standards and enhancing quality between two or more organisations to deliver aspects of teaching, learning, assessment and student support.

Further education and technical and vocational qualification resources

Recruit further education (FE) teachers from overseas (FE)

Guidance on ensuring all individuals working with children have the relevant employment and criminal record checks.

Further education and skills inspection toolkit (FE)

This toolkit sets out the areas that will be evaluated and graded on inspections of providers of further education and skills under part 8 of the Education and Inspections Act 2006. It can also be used by leaders to support self-evaluation and continuous improvement.

College financial handbook (FE)

Guidance for college governors, accounting officers, chief financial officers, governance professionals and auditors.

Ofqual handbook: general conditions of recognition (FE)

Rules and guidance for recognised awarding organisations in England, including governance, risk management, third-party arrangements, qualification delivery, assessment, complaints and withdrawal.

Regulation – qualifications Wales (FE in Wales)

Regulatory framework and requirements for recognised awarding bodies and qualifications offered to learners in Wales, including relevant conditions, procedures and policies.

Qualifications Scotland Accreditation – regulation (FE in Scotland)

Regulatory framework for approved awarding bodies and accredited qualifications in Scotland, including compliance requirements, audit, provider monitoring and risk-based oversight.

Qualifications framework – The Council for Curriculum, Examinations and Assessment (FE in Northern Ireland)

Information on regulated qualifications in Northern Ireland, including the Regulated Qualifications Framework, recognition requirements and comparison of qualification levels across the UK, Ireland and Europe.

School-specific resources

British schools overseas: standards for school (schools overseas)

Standards used in the voluntary British schools overseas accreditation scheme, including quality, safeguarding and governance expectations.

Keeping children safe in education 2026: September 2026 (schools)

Schools and colleges in England must have regard to this when carrying out their duties to safeguard and promote the welfare of children. Part Three of the guidance has four sections providing schools and colleges with the legal requirements ‘must’ do, what they ‘should’ do, what is considered best practice and important information about Safer Recruitment.

Research-specific resources

National Protective Security Authority (NPSA) Trust Research (research and HE)

Practical guidance and tools for due diligence, collaboration, travel, governance, protecting people, research and intellectual property.

NPSA Trusted Research: countries and conferences (research and HE)

Risk considerations for overseas travel, conferences, local laws, data, devices and research engagement.

Research Collaboration Advice Team (research institutions)

Direct, tailored government advice to research institutions on national security risks in international research collaboration.

National and economic security compliance and guidance

National Security and Investment Act: guidance for higher education and research (HE and research)

How the National Security and Investment Act may apply to acquisitions, control and relevant collaborations in HE and research-intensive activity.

Foreign Influence Registration Scheme: guidance from academia and research (HE and research)

Sector-specific guidance on whether arrangements and activities require registration under the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme.

Export controls applying to academic research (research and HE)

How strategic export controls can apply to research, technology, software, data, teaching and technical assistance.

UK strategic export controls (all providers where controlled items or technology may be involved)

General guidance, control-list and end-user tools, licensing and Export Control Joint Unit support.

Information Commissioner’s Office guidance on international transfers (all providers)

Identifying restricted transfers and selecting safeguards, transfer risk assessments and contractual measures under UK GDPR.

Academic Technology Approval Scheme (HE and research)

Requirements for certain foreign students and researchers studying or conducting research in sensitive technology-related fields in the UK.

Transnational repression (all providers)

Practical advice on how to safeguard yourself if you are concerned about transnational repression or believe yourself to be a victim.

Bribery Act 2010 guidance (all providers)

Guidance to help commercial organisations understand the sorts of procedures they can put in place to prevent bribery.

UK Export Finance: The UK’s export credit agency (all providers)

Government-backed export finance, working-capital guarantees and insurance that may help UK providers win and fulfil overseas contracts and manage the risk of buyer default.

Suspicious Activity Reports – National Crime Agency

Suspicious activity reports (SARs) alert law enforcement to potential instances of money laundering or terrorist financing.

Charity resources

Charities: how to manage risks when working internationally (registered charities)

Guidance for charities in England and Wales on assessing overseas risks, protecting staff and beneficiaries, checking local partners, and safeguarding money and other resources.

Managing conflicts of interest in a charity (registered charities)

Guidance for charities in England and Wales on identifying, declaring, managing and recording conflicts of interest that could affect trustee decision-making.

Cyber security resources

Report a Cyber Incident - National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) (all providers)

UK government signposting and reporting route for cyber incidents, including where multiple organisations may need to be notified.

NCSC cyber security for education (HE and FE)

Cyber security guidance and practical resources for higher and further education; use relevant NCSC education resources for other provider types.
